metaDescription: Six home Ethernet switches compared on port count, gigabit versus 2.5G, unmanaged versus Easy Smart, PoE budget and metal fanless builds for desks and closets.
expertTake: The NETGEAR GS308 8-port is the best overall pick because it gives enough ports for a typical home, a fanless design and plug-and-play setup. The TP-Link TL-SG105 5-port is the value pick for a desk or TV console that needs a few extra wired connections. Skip a new switch if your router already has spare gigabit ports, because an extra box adds a point of failure without adding speed.
introParagraphs: An Ethernet switch turns one wired connection into several, which is useful when a router runs out of ports for a desktop, a console, a streaming box and a printer. A switch does not add internet speed, but it keeps wired devices on a faster and more stable link than Wi-Fi.

For most homes an unmanaged gigabit switch is all you need. The differences are port count, build quality, whether it supports 2.5 gigabit or power over Ethernet and whether it has any management features. The six switches below cover each of those needs.

products.name: NETGEAR GS308 8-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Ethernet Switch
products.description:
The NETGEAR GS308 is the most sensible home switch: eight gigabit ports in a small desktop box, with plug-and-play operation and no software. Its ports auto-negotiate speed, so older 100 megabit devices and modern gigabit devices coexist without setup. The 8-port count covers a desktop, a console, a TV, a streaming box, a printer and a couple of spares.

Compared with the TP-Link TL-SG105, the GS308 has three more ports for a small cost increase, which is usually worth it because networks grow. Against the GS308E Easy Smart model it lacks VLANs and monitoring, but it is simpler and cheaper. It is a pure expander: it does not add internet speed, so the router link remains the shared limit.

Place it where it can breathe, connect the uplink to the router and plug in devices. Use Cat5e or better cables, and check the port LEDs if a link seems slow. A fanless design means silence. For a home that needs a few more wired connections, this is the safe pick.
products.bestFor: Homes that need eight wired ports with no setup.
pros: Eight gigabit ports cover a typical home
Plug and play with no software
Auto-negotiating ports handle mixed speeds
Desktop or wall mounting
cons: Shares one gigabit uplink to the router

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105 5-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Ethernet Switch, Metal
products.description:
The TP-Link TL-SG105 is the small, cheap desk switch: five gigabit ports in a fanless metal case with plug-and-play setup. The listing mentions an energy-efficient design that lowers power draw on idle ports and IEEE 802.3X flow control to keep transfers steady. One port goes to the router and four serve devices.

Compared with the NETGEAR GS308, it has fewer ports at a lower cost, which suits a TV console or a desk with three or four wired devices. Against the LS1005G LiteWave from the same brand, the metal case here is sturdier and the housing dissipates heat better. For most people a five-port switch is enough until they add a camera or a second console.

Connect the uplink to the router and plug in devices. If you see a link at 100 Mbps, replace the cable, since a damaged pair will drop the speed. Keep it dry and ventilated, and use the included power adapter rather than a spare one with a different rating, since an undersized adapter causes the random link drops that people blame on the switch. For a single desk or entertainment center, it is the best value pick.
products.bestFor: Desks and TV consoles that need a few extra wired ports at low cost.
pros: Five gigabit ports in a small metal case
Fanless so it runs silently
Energy-efficient port design
Low cost and plug and play
cons: Only four usable ports after the uplink
Fills up quickly as devices are added

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG105S-M2 5-Port 2.5G Multi-Gigabit Unmanaged Switch
products.description:
The TL-SG105S-M2 is a five-port multi-gigabit switch with every port running at up to 2.5 Gbps, and the ports auto-negotiate down to gigabit and slower for older devices. It is aimed at home entertainment, LAN parties and fast file transfers between a desktop and a NAS, where a 2.5G link can move data faster than a gigabit connection.

Compared with the TP-Link TL-SG105, it costs noticeably more for the same port count. The extra speed only helps if both ends of a link run at 2.5G, such as a motherboard with a 2.5G port and a NAS, or a router with a 2.5G LAN port. Against the NETGEAR GS308 it offers more speed but fewer ports, so it is a targeted upgrade, not a general one.

Use Cat5e or better cabling, since Cat5e handles 2.5G at typical home lengths. Check which of your devices actually have 2.5G ports before paying for them. The uplink to the router is the shared limit, so a gigabit router still caps outside access. For a desktop and NAS pair, it is an effective upgrade.
products.bestFor: People with 2.5G devices or a NAS who want faster local transfers.
pros: All five ports run at up to 2.5 Gbps
Auto-negotiates down to gigabit
Plug and play with no software
Fanless desktop or wall design
cons: Only helps if both ends support 2.5G

products.name: NETGEAR GS308E 8-Port Gigabit Easy Smart Managed Switch
products.description:
The GS308E is an Easy Smart switch: it works out of the box like an unmanaged unit, but a web GUI on Windows, Mac or Linux adds VLANs, port monitoring and segmentation. That is useful if you want to separate IoT devices or cameras from your computers, or to see which port is carrying traffic.

Compared with the NETGEAR GS308, the same 8 ports with a management layer cost a little more. Against the TP-Link Easy Smart 8-port model it provides a similar feature set from a familiar brand. Most homes do not need any of it, so choose this only if you plan to build VLANs or want visibility into traffic.

If you do use the GUI, set a static IP for the switch, label VLANs clearly and keep a backup of the configuration. Leave the defaults for a normal home network. The tradeoff is added complexity for a benefit that many people never use. For a tinkerer who wants a safe step into managed networking, it is a good starting point.
products.bestFor: Tinkerers who want VLANs and traffic visibility on a simple switch.
pros: Easy Smart web GUI on any desktop OS
VLAN support for IoT and cameras
Works plug and play without setup
Eight gigabit ports
cons: Costs more than the plain unmanaged GS308
Management features go unused by most homes
A mistake in VLANs can lock you out

products.name: NETGEAR GS305P 5-Port PoE Gigabit Unmanaged Switch, 4 PoE+ Ports 63W
products.description:
The GS305P is a five-port switch with four PoE+ ports sharing a 63 watt total power budget, plus dynamic allocation that assigns power to devices based on need. PoE lets a single Ethernet cable carry both data and power to an IP camera, a wireless access point or a VoIP phone, so you avoid a power adapter at each location.

The limit is the shared budget: four PoE+ ports can each supply up to 30 watts, but the total is 63 watts, so you cannot run four high-draw devices at full load. Compared with the plain NETGEAR GS305, it costs more, and it makes sense only if you have a PoE device. For a few IP cameras, which draw under 10 watts each, it is ample.

Check the power rating of each PoE device and add them up. Use quality cables, since poor cables waste power and limit speed. Mount it in a cool spot, since PoE adds heat. For a home with cameras or an access point on the ceiling, it solves a wiring problem with one box.
products.bestFor: Homes with IP cameras or access points that need power over Ethernet.
pros: Four PoE+ ports power cameras and access points
63 W total budget with dynamic allocation
Unmanaged plug and play
One cable carries data and power
cons: Shared 63 W budget limits high-draw devices
Costs more than a non-PoE switch

products.name: TP-Link TL-SG116 16-Port Gigabit Unmanaged Switch, Metal Fanless
products.description:
The TL-SG116 is the answer for a home that has outgrown eight ports: sixteen gigabit ports in a fanless metal case with shielded ports and desktop or wall mounting. It suits a wiring closet, a home office with many devices or a house wired room by room.

Compared with the NETGEAR GS308, it doubles the ports without adding fan noise. Against a 24-port switch it is smaller and easier to place, which matters if you have no rack. Even with 16 ports, the single uplink to the router is a shared pipe, so heavy traffic from many devices at once shares one gigabit link.

Label each cable, use a short cable run from the router and keep the unit in a ventilated spot. A metal case acts as a heatsink, so avoid stacking it under warm gear. If you have many wired rooms, this is the right size.
products.bestFor: Homes wired room by room that need many ports in one place.
pros: Sixteen gigabit ports in one box
Fanless metal case runs silently
Shielded ports and wall mount option
Room for growth
cons: All ports share one uplink to the router
Larger than the 5 and 8 port switches

buyingCriteria.criterion: Port count with room to grow
buyingCriteria.explanation: Count the devices you will plug in and add two spare ports, because networks grow. Five ports serve a desk, eight cover a typical home and sixteen suit a room-by-room install. The TL-SG105 has five, the GS308 has eight and the TL-SG116 has sixteen. One port is taken by the uplink to the router. A common mistake is buying the exact count and then daisy-chaining a second switch later, which adds another box and another power adapter; paying a little more for the 8-port GS308 up front usually avoids that.

A gigabit switch is enough for most homes, because a typical internet plan and Wi-Fi are slower than 1 Gbps. A 2.5G switch like the TL-SG105S-M2 only helps when both ends of a link support 2.5G, such as a NAS and a desktop. Do not pay for 2.5G if your devices lack 2.5G ports. Also check the router side: if the router only has gigabit LAN ports, a 2.5G switch can still speed up transfers between two local 2.5G devices, but internet traffic leaving the house is capped by the gigabit uplink.

Unmanaged switches work out of the box with no setup, while Easy Smart switches add VLANs and monitoring through a web page. The GS308 is unmanaged and the GS308E is Easy Smart. For most homes unmanaged is enough, and management is a niche need for camera or IoT separation.

PoE switches carry power to cameras and access points over the same cable, but the budget is shared across ports. The GS305P gives four PoE+ ports on a 63 W total. Add up your devices' draw before buying, because a low budget switches off ports under load. As a worked example, three cameras drawing about 7 watts each use roughly 21 watts of the GS305P's 63 watt budget, leaving room for an access point on the fourth PoE+ port.

Metal fanless housings dissipate heat silently, while plastic cases run warmer. The TP-Link and NETGEAR picks here are fanless. Place the switch where air can move around it and avoid stacking it under warm gear.

All devices on the switch share the single link back to the router. A bigger switch does not make the connection faster. For heavy local transfers, connect busy devices to the same switch so traffic stays local. Use Cat5e or better cabling.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ports and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared port counts and speed tiers against typical home needs. The GS308 and TL-SG116 lead for ports, and the TL-SG105S-M2 leads for speed. We separated gigabit from 2.5G.

howWeEvaluated.title: Management features
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared unmanaged and Easy Smart switches and the value of VLANs. The GS308E adds management at a small cost. Unmanaged switches were credited for simplicity.

howWeEvaluated.title: PoE and power
howWeEvaluated.description: We read PoE budgets and per-port limits. The GS305P's 63 W budget was judged against typical camera loads. Non-PoE switches were judged on need.

howWeEvaluated.title: Build and cooling
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at metal housings, fanless design and mounting options. The TP-Link metal cases and NETGEAR housings earned credit. Silence mattered for desk use.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership and reliability
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed owner feedback patterns on port failures, noise and power adapters. Fanless metal builds fared well. Shared uplink limits were noted.

maintenance.why: A port that links at 100 Mbps often has a bad cable. Replace the cable to restore gigabit.
Dust traps heat even on fanless metal cases. Wipe the housing.
A failing adapter causes random drops. Replace it with the same rating.
Labels make troubleshooting a closet fast.
Easy Smart settings can be lost on reset. Save the configuration.

faq.q: Does an Ethernet switch slow my network?
faq.a: No. A gigabit switch passes traffic at line rate. Devices share the uplink to the router, so heavy use on several devices can saturate that link.

faq.q: Do I need a managed switch?
faq.a: Rarely. Unmanaged is enough for most homes, and Easy Smart is useful for VLANs or cameras.
Only if both ends of a link support 2.5G, like a NAS and a desktop. Otherwise gigabit is enough.

faq.q: How many ports should I buy?
faq.a: Count your devices, add two spare ports and remember one port is the uplink. Eight ports suit most homes.
Power over Ethernet sends power and data on one cable. The GS305P has four PoE+ ports with a 63 W total budget.
Cat5e supports gigabit and 2.5G at home lengths, and Cat6 is a safe choice. A bad cable drops the link speed.
